A: Kṛṣṇa's teaching of knowledge with vijñāna of himself 'entire'. Movements: (1) 7.1–3 announcement — with mind attached to him and taking refuge, Arjuna will know him fully; knowledge with vijñāna after which nothing remains to be known; the rarity of those who know him in truth. (2) 7.4–7 his two natures: the lower eightfold prakṛti (five elements, mind, intellect, I-maker) and the higher prakṛti that has become the living being and upholds the world; both are the source of beings; he is the origin and dissolution of all; nothing is higher; all is strung on him like gems on a thread. (3) 7.8–12 he as the essence in things (taste in water, light of sun and moon, Oṃ in the Vedas, life, austerity, intelligence, strength, desire not opposed to dharma); the states of the three guṇas come from him, he is not in them, they in him. (4) 7.13–15 the world deluded by the guṇas does not know him; his divine guṇa-made māyā is crossed by those who take refuge in him; evil-doers of demonic disposition do not. (5) 7.16–19 four kinds of virtuous worshippers (distressed, seeker of knowledge, seeker of gain, knower); the knower, of single devotion, is foremost and held to be his very self; after many births the knower takes refuge, knowing 'Vāsudeva is all'. (6) 7.20–23 those driven by desires worship other deities; he makes their faith firm and grants the fruit, which is finite; god-worshippers go to the gods, his devotees to him. (7) 7.24–26 the unintelligent take the unmanifest as merely manifest; he is veiled by yoga-māyā; he knows all beings, none knows him. (8) 7.27–30 beings are bewildered by the pairs from birth; those whose sin has ended worship him; those striving for release from old age and death know Brahman, adhyātma and karma, and those who know him with adhibhūta, adhidaiva and adhiyajña know him even at death — terms that lead into chapter 8. Purpose as the chapter presents it: complete knowledge of the Lord, and refuge in him as the way across his māyā.
B: Chapter 7 (in colophons 'jñāna-vijñāna-yoga'): Kṛṣṇa undertakes to teach how Arjuna, mind fixed on him and taking refuge in him, will know him entirely (7.1–2), noting the rarity of such knowers (7.3). Movements: (1) 7.4–7 his two natures — the lower eightfold prakṛti (elements, mind, intellect, I-making) and the higher one that has become the living being; he is the origin and dissolution of the world, nothing is higher, all is strung on him; (2) 7.8–12 he is the essence in things (taste in water, light of sun and moon, Oṃ in the Vedas, the eternal seed, desire not opposed to dharma); the guṇa-states come from him, yet he is not in them; (3) 7.13–15 the world, deluded by the guṇa-made divine māyā, does not know him; only those who take refuge in him cross it; evil-doers of demonic disposition do not; (4) 7.16–19 four kinds of virtuous worshippers — afflicted, inquirer, seeker of wealth, knower — the knower being his very self, the rare great soul who after many births knows 'Vāsudeva is all'; (5) 7.20–23 those whose knowledge is stolen by desires worship other deities; he steadies their faith and grants their finite fruits; (6) 7.24–26 the unintelligent misjudge his unmanifest supreme state; veiled by yoga-māyā he is not manifest to all; he knows all beings, none knows him; (7) 7.27–30 beings are bewildered by the pairs born of desire and aversion; the meritorious, freed from them, worship him, and those who strive for release know brahman, adhyātma, karma, adhibhūta, adhidaiva and adhiyajña, and know him at the time of departure — terms that lead into chapter 8.
resolution: merged: Chapter 7 moves in eight steps. (1) 7.1–3: with his mind attached to the Lord, practising yoga and taking refuge in him, Arjuna will know him entirely (samagram) and without doubt; the Lord will declare knowledge together with vijñāna, after which nothing further remains to be known; among thousands scarcely one strives for perfection, and of those who strive scarcely one knows him in truth. (2) 7.4–7: his two natures — the lower, divided eightfold (earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of 'I'), and the higher, which has become the living being and by which the world is upheld; all beings have these two as their womb; he is the origin and the dissolution of the whole world; nothing is higher than him, and all this is strung on him like gems on a thread. (3) 7.8–12: he is the essence in things — the taste in water, the light of moon and sun, Oṃ in all the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men, fragrance in earth, brilliance in fire, life in all beings, austerity in ascetics, the eternal seed of beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the strength of the strong free of desire and passion, desire not opposed to dharma; the states of sattva, rajas and tamas come from him, yet he is not in them — they are in him. (4) 7.13–15: deluded by these guṇa-made states the world does not know him; his divine māyā made of the guṇas is hard to cross, but those who take refuge in him alone cross it; evil-doers of demonic disposition, their knowledge carried off by māyā, do not take refuge in him. (5) 7.16–19: four kinds of people of good deeds worship him — the distressed, the one who wishes to know, the seeker of gain and the knower; all are noble, but the knower, ever yoked and of single devotion, is foremost, mutually dear with him and held by him to be his very self; at the end of many births the knower takes refuge in him, knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' — a great soul very hard to find. (6) 7.20–23: those whose knowledge desires have carried off resort to other deities, following their observances; whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, he makes that faith firm, and through it the worshipper obtains desires ordained by him; but the fruit is finite — worshippers of the gods go to the gods, his devotees come to him. (7) 7.24–26: the unintelligent think him, the unmanifest, to have come into manifestation, not knowing his higher, imperishable state; veiled by his yoga-māyā he is not manifest to all; he knows all beings past, present and to come, but no one knows him. (8) 7.27–30: all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs born of desire and aversion; those of meritorious deeds whose sin has ended worship him firm in their vows; those who take refuge in him and strive for release from old age and death know Brahman, the adhyātma and action completely, and those who know him with the adhibhūta, the adhidaiva and the adhiyajña know him even at the time of departure — terms that Arjuna asks about in 8.1–2. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to give the knowledge of the Lord 'entire' (samagra), together with vijñāna, and to show refuge in him as the way across his māyā.
reason: the two chapter summaries agree on the movements (A: 7.1-3 as a first movement and eight in all; B: 7.1-3 as preamble and seven); merged on A's division with B's details (the eternal seed, the fruits ordained by the Lord), both purposes kept (A: refuge in him as the way across his maya; B: knowing him entirely)

A: Answers to Arjuna's questions about the terms of 7.29–30 and about knowing the Lord at death; the imperishable (akṣara) as the goal. Movements: (1) 8.1–2 Arjuna asks what Brahman, adhyātma, karma, adhibhūta, adhidaiva and adhiyajña are, and how the Lord is known at the time of departure. (2) 8.3–4 definitions: Brahman is the supreme imperishable, adhyātma its own being, karma the emission that brings beings into existence, adhibhūta the perishable state, adhidaivata the Person, adhiyajña the Lord himself in the body. (3) 8.5–8 whoever dies remembering him comes to his state; one goes to whatever one remembers at the end, as habitually dwelt on; so remember him always and fight; constant practice leads to the supreme Person. (4) 8.9–13 the dying yogin's meditation: on the ancient seer beyond darkness, with breath between the brows; the imperishable 'state' declared in brief; restraining the gates, mind in the heart, breath in the head, uttering Oṃ and remembering him, one reaches the supreme goal. (5) 8.14–16 he is easy to reach for the constant rememberer; those who reach him are not reborn, whereas all worlds up to Brahmā's return. (6) 8.17–22 Brahmā's day and night of a thousand ages; beings manifest from and dissolve into the unmanifest; beyond it another eternal unmanifest, called the imperishable, the supreme goal and his supreme abode, reached by undivided devotion to the all-pervading Person. (7) 8.23–27 the two courses of the departed: the bright (fire, light, day, bright fortnight, northern half-year) leading to Brahman without return, the dark (smoke, night, dark fortnight, southern half-year) leading to the lunar light and return; the yogin who knows them is not deluded. (8) 8.28 the yogin who knows this passes beyond all merit of Veda, sacrifice, austerity and gift to the supreme primal place.
B: Chapter 8 (in colophons 'akṣara-brahma-yoga') answers the terms left open at 7.29–30. Movements: (1) 8.1–2 Arjuna asks seven questions — what are brahman, adhyātma, karma, adhibhūta, adhidaiva, who is the adhiyajña in this body, and how is the Lord known at the time of departure; (2) 8.3–4 definitions: brahman is the supreme imperishable, adhyātma its own being, karma the sending-forth that makes beings arise, adhibhūta perishable being, adhidaivata the Person, adhiyajña the Lord himself in the body; (3) 8.5–8 whoever dies remembering him attains his state; one goes to whatever one remembers at the end, so remember him always and fight, with the mind held by practice; (4) 8.9–13 the meditation at departure: remembering the ancient seer beyond darkness, with steady mind, devotion and yoga-power, breath between the brows; gates restrained, mind in the heart, breath in the head, uttering Oṃ and remembering him — reaching the supreme goal; (5) 8.14–16 he is easy to reach for the constantly remembering yogin; those who reach him are not reborn, while all worlds up to Brahmā's return; (6) 8.17–19 the day and night of Brahmā, each a thousand yugas, in which beings emerge from and dissolve into the unmanifest; (7) 8.20–22 beyond that unmanifest is another eternal unmanifest, the imperishable, the highest goal and his supreme abode, the supreme Person attained by undivided devotion; (8) 8.23–27 the two paths of departing yogins — the bright (fire, light, day, bright fortnight, northern course) to brahman without return, the dark (smoke, night, dark fortnight, southern course) to the lunar light and return — and knowing them the yogin is not deluded; (9) 8.28 the yogin who knows this surpasses all the merit of Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts and reaches the supreme primal abode.
resolution: merged: Chapter 8 moves in nine steps. (1) 8.1–2: Arjuna asks seven questions — what is that Brahman, what is the adhyātma, what is action, what are the adhibhūta and the adhidaiva, who and how is the adhiyajña here in the body, and how is the Lord to be known at the time of departure by the self-controlled. (2) 8.3–4: the Lord's answers: Brahman is the supreme imperishable; own being (svabhāva) is called the adhyātma; the sending-forth (visarga) that brings about beings' states of existence is called action; the adhibhūta is the perishable state, the adhidaivata the Person (puruṣa), and the adhiyajña the Lord himself, here in the body. (3) 8.5–8: whoever departs at the end remembering him alone comes to his state; one goes to whatever state one remembers on leaving the body, having always been shaped by it; therefore Arjuna is to remember him at all times and fight, with mind and intellect offered to him; with a mind yoked by the yoga of repeated practice one goes to the supreme divine Person. (4) 8.9–13: the departure of one who remembers: whoever at departure, with unmoving mind, devotion and the power of yoga, the breath made to enter between the brows, remembers the ancient seer, subtler than the subtle, sun-coloured, beyond darkness, reaches that supreme divine Person; the imperishable that knowers of the Veda speak of and ascetics enter is declared in brief: whoever departs having restrained the gates, confined the mind in the heart and placed the breath in the head, uttering Oṃ, the one-syllabled Brahman, and remembering him, goes to the supreme goal. (5) 8.14–16: for the ever-yoked yogin who remembers him constantly with undivided mind he is easy to reach; the great souls who come to him are not reborn into the impermanent abode of sorrow, whereas all worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return. (6) 8.17–19: Brahmā's day lasts a thousand yugas and his night as long; at the coming of day manifest things come forth from the unmanifest, at the coming of night they dissolve into it, and the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly. (7) 8.20–22: beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest being that does not perish when all beings perish; it is called the imperishable and the supreme goal, from which they do not return — his supreme abode; that supreme Person, in whom beings abide and by whom all is pervaded, is gained by undivided devotion. (8) 8.23–27: the times at which departing yogins go to non-return or to return: fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the six months of the northern course lead the knowers of Brahman to Brahman; smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the six months of the southern course lead the yogin to the lunar light and return; these two courses are everlasting for the world, and knowing them no yogin is deluded — so Arjuna is to be yoked in yoga at all times. (9) 8.28: having known this, the yogin goes beyond all the merit declared for the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities and gifts and reaches the supreme, primal place. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer the questions left open at 7.29–30, above all how the Lord is known at death, and to show that constant remembrance of him, carried through to the moment of departure, leads to the imperishable from which there is no return.
reason: the two summaries agree in substance (A eight movements, B nine); merged on B's division (8.17-19 and 8.20-22 apart) with A's wording where fuller; neither states a purpose, so one is given from the chapter's own frame (8.1-2 questions, 8.5-7 and 8.28 results)

A: The 'royal knowledge, royal secret': the Lord's pervasion and transcendence of the world, and devotion as the way open to all. Movements: (1) 9.1–3 the most secret knowledge with vijñāna, for one free of cavilling; praised as royal knowledge, purifying, directly known, easy; those without faith return to death and saṃsāra. (2) 9.4–10 the Lord pervades all in unmanifest form; beings abide in him but he not in them — and yet beings do not abide in him: his lordly yoga; the wind in space as illustration; at the end of a kalpa beings enter his prakṛti and he sends them forth again; those acts do not bind him, seated as if indifferent; prakṛti produces the world under his oversight. (3) 9.11–15 the deluded, of demonic nature, disregard him in human form; the great-souled of divine nature worship him with undivided mind, glorifying and bowing, or through the sacrifice of knowledge as one, distinct and many. (4) 9.16–19 he is every element of the sacrifice, father and mother of the world, Oṃ and the three Vedas, goal, witness, refuge, friend, origin and dissolution, immortality and death, being and non-being. (5) 9.20–25 Vedic ritualists win heaven and return when merit is spent; the undivided devotee's welfare he carries himself; worship of other deities reaches him but not by the rule; each goes to what he worships. (6) 9.26–34 the simplest offering (leaf, flower, fruit, water) is accepted; doing all as an offering to him frees from the bonds of action; he is the same to all yet devotees are in him and he in them; even one of very bad conduct who worships undividedly is to be counted good and does not perish; women, vaiśyas, śūdras and those of sinful birth reach the highest goal by refuge in him; closing injunction: mind on me, my devotee, my worshipper, bow to me, you will come to me.
B: Chapter 9 (in colophons 'rājavidyā-rājaguhya-yoga') resumes the knowledge-with-vijñāna of 7.2 as the most secret, royal knowledge. Movements: (1) 9.1–3 announcement to the non-carping Arjuna: royal knowledge, royal secret, directly evident, easy to practise; the faithless return to death-and-wandering; (2) 9.4–10 the Lord and beings: he pervades all in unmanifest form, beings are in him and he not in them — and yet they are not in him (his sovereign yoga); like wind in space; at the end of a kalpa beings enter his prakṛti and he sends them forth again, unbound by these acts, sitting as if indifferent, prakṛti bearing the world under his oversight; (3) 9.11–12 the deluded disregard him in human form, resorting to a demonic, deluding nature; (4) 9.13–15 great souls of divine nature worship him single-mindedly — singing his praise, striving, bowing — and others by the sacrifice of knowledge; (5) 9.16–19 he is the rite, the sacrifice, the fire and the oblation, father and mother of the world, Oṃ and the three Vedas, the goal, witness, refuge and friend, immortality and death, sat and asat; (6) 9.20–21 the Vedic sacrificers reach Indra's heaven and return when their merit is spent; (7) 9.22–25 he bears the gain and security of undivided worshippers; worshippers of other deities worship him not by rule and fall, each going to what he worships; (8) 9.26–28 any offering given in devotion, even a leaf, he accepts; every act is to be offered to him, freeing from the bonds of action; (9) 9.29–34 he is the same to all yet dwells in his devotees; even the very ill-conducted who worships him is to be deemed good; his devotee does not perish; those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras reach the highest goal, how much more brāhmaṇas and royal sages; closing injunction: mind on me, devotion, sacrifice and homage to me, and you will come to me.
resolution: merged: Chapter 9 moves in nine steps. (1) 9.1–3: to Arjuna, who does not cavil, the Lord will declare the most secret knowledge together with vijñāna, knowing which he will be freed from what is inauspicious — the royal knowledge, the royal secret, the supreme purifier, directly apprehended, in accord with dharma, very easy to practise, imperishable; those without faith in this dharma do not reach him and return to the path of death and saṃsāra. (2) 9.4–10: all this is pervaded by him in unmanifest form; all beings abide in him, but he is not established in them — and yet beings do not abide in him: 'behold my lordly yoga'; his self sustains beings and brings them into being without abiding in them, as the great wind always abides in space; at the close of a kalpa beings go into his prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth again, taking hold of his own prakṛti; these acts do not bind him, seated as one indifferent and unattached; with him as overseer prakṛti gives birth to the moving and the unmoving, and so the world revolves. (3) 9.11–12: the deluded disregard him who has taken on a human body, not knowing his higher state as the great Lord of beings; of vain hopes, vain acts and vain knowledge, they resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras. (4) 9.13–15: the great souls, resorting to the divine nature, worship him with minds on nothing else — always glorifying him, striving, firm in their vows, bowing to him with devotion, ever yoked — and others worship him by the sacrifice of knowledge, as one, as distinct and in many ways. (5) 9.16–19: he is the rite, the sacrifice, the offering to the ancestors, the healing plant, the mantra, the clarified butter, the fire and the oblation; the father, mother, sustainer and grandsire of the world, what is to be known, the purifier, Oṃ, and the Ṛk, Sāman and Yajus; the goal, upholder, lord, witness, dwelling, refuge and friend, the origin, dissolution, ground, treasure-house and imperishable seed; he gives heat, holds back and sends forth the rain; he is immortality and death, being and non-being. (6) 9.20–21: knowers of the three Vedas who have worshipped him with sacrifices pray for heaven, enjoy the world of the lord of the gods and, their merit spent, enter the world of mortals again — 'going and coming'. (7) 9.22–25: for those who, having no other, think of him and worship him, ever devoted, he himself carries acquisition and preservation; devotees of other deities who sacrifice with faith sacrifice to him, but not according to the rule; not recognising him in truth as the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices, they fall; those vowed to the gods, the ancestors or the spirits go to them, and those who sacrifice to him come to him. (8) 9.26–28: a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water offered with devotion he partakes of; whatever Arjuna does, eats, offers, gives or practises as austerity is to be done as an offering to him, and so he will be freed from the bonds of action with their good and bad fruits and, yoked in the yoga of renunciation, will come to him. (9) 9.29–34: he is the same to all beings, none hateful or dear to him, but those who worship him with devotion are in him and he in them; even one of very bad conduct who worships him with undivided devotion is to be considered good and quickly becomes righteous — his devotee does not perish; those who take refuge in him, even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras, go to the highest goal, how much more holy brāhmaṇas and devoted royal seers; closing injunction: having come to this impermanent, joyless world, worship him — mind on him, his devotee, sacrificing to him, bowing to him — and Arjuna will come to him. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to resume the knowledge with vijñāna of 7.2 as the 'royal knowledge, royal secret' — the Lord who pervades all this and yet is not contained in it — and to present devotion to him, open to all who take refuge, as the way to him.
